title: Göbekli Tepe and 8 Other Ancient Sites Every Design Lover Should Visit
excerpt: From rock-cut Nabataean tombs to monolithic subterranean temples, these extraordinary ruins prove humanity's spatial imagination has always exceeded expectations
content:
Since humanity's earliest history, we have been driven by a primal urge to carve drama into the earth. Whether it's the 11,500-year-old pillars of Göbekli Tepe that shattered our understanding of early architecture, or the monolithic wonders sculpted straight into living rock across the ancient Arab and Roman worlds, these elemental monuments remain our most evocative structural legacy.

The human urge to build things is nothing new. The rise of Rome, the pharaonic dynasties, the marble colonnades of classical antiquity. Era after era, empires left behind grand stone monuments to mark their peak, and for decades, we operated on the neat assumption that humans first had to farm, settle, and build towns before they could ever muster the collective labour needed for design at such a large scale.

That neat chronology fell apart in the mid-1990s when archaeologists started unearthing a quiet hilltop in southeastern Türkiye known as Göbekli Tepe. Dating back roughly 11,500 years, the excavation revealed massive ringed enclosures anchored by T-shaped stone pillars, some standing up to 18 feet tall and weighing up to 15 tons. But what makes the discovery even more incredible is its timeline. Within just a couple of years of analysing the flint tools, animal bones and early radiocarbon dates, the team confirmed that the monumental pillars were carved by nomadic hunter-gatherers during the Pre-Pottery Neolithic era, well before domestic farming or metal tools existed.

Across the globe, similar ancient sites offer a window into this primal design instinct, where master builders worked without modern tools to achieve scale. Below, we look at eight extraordinary architectural wonders to experience up close.

Hegra (Mada'in Salih), Saudi Arabia

First on our list is Hegra, an ancient trade hub set in the desert plains of AlUla in northwestern Saudi Arabia. As the second city of the Nabataean Kingdom after Petra, it holds the distinction of being Saudi Arabia’s very first UNESCO World Heritage Site, dating to the 1st century AD. Rather than building upward with quarried stone, Nabataean architects used a purely subtractive approach, working from the top down to create 100 monumental tombs directly into isolated sandstone cliffs. Masons sculpted elaborate facades complete with Hellenistic porticos, Roman columns and step motifs straight into living rock. The site's defining moment, Qasr al-Farid, rises four stories out of the golden sand; a solitary masterpiece of ancient craftsmanship.

Baalbek, Lebanon

To understand the absolute upper limit of Roman engineering, look to the staggering scale of Baalbek, set in the fertile Beqaa Valley of eastern Lebanon, roughly 85 kilometres northeast of Beirut. Known in antiquity as Heliopolis, or the “City of the Sun,” this expansive sanctuary features the celebrated Temple of Bacchus, widely regarded as the best-preserved Roman temple interior in the world. But its most mind-boggling feature lies beneath the adjacent sanctuary terrace, where archaeologists found a foundation wall anchored by the “Trilithon”, a legendary trio of massive limestone blocks weighing roughly 800 tons each.

Persepolis, Iran

Set on the windswept plains of southwestern Iran, near modern-day Shiraz, Persepolis was built to project the absolute majesty of the First Persian Empire. Commissioned in 515 BC by Darius the Great, the ceremonial capital was raised on a massive artificial terrace spanning 125,000 square meters. Architecturally, the complex combines Egyptian stonemasonry, Babylonian relief work and Greek column proportions into a singular Achaemenid style. Alexander the Great may have looted and burned it down in 330 BC, but the city’s stone bones held up remarkably well. Today, walking through the Gate of All Nations or the relief-adorned Apadana Palace reveals a monumental landscape of towering columns, carved staircases and soaring stone gateways.

Regio IX, Pompeii, Italy

Few archaeological sites offer a real-time snapshot of ancient interior design quite like Pompeii's Regio IX district. Recent digs in this previously unexplored neighbourhood have unveiled remarkably intact Roman domestic life, from commercial bakeries and thermal baths to sophisticated private residences. The standout discovery is a grand banquet hall painted with deep black walls (a clever architectural trick designed to absorb torch soot during evening dinner parties) framed by vibrant mythological frescoes. More than just a site of tragedy and plaster casts, which are just as striking to see in person, Regio IX is a living gallery of ancient interior design, demonstrating a masterful use of colour, mood lighting and practical layout.

Ziggurat of Ur, Iraq

A massive, stepped mud-brick mountain rising against the horizon, the Ziggurat of Ur sits in the desert plains of southern Iraq, roughly 15 kilometres from modern-day Nasiriyah. Built around 2100 BC by King Ur-Nammu, this sacred Neo-Sumerian complex served as both an administrative hub and a temple dedicated to the moon god Nanna. While ongoing restoration efforts protect the Ziggurat of Ur from harsh climate erosion, its ancient engineering remains brilliantly adaptive: a core of sun-dried mud bricks was encased in a thick shell of fired bricks set with natural bitumen. Masons even built the outer walls with subtle outward curves to correct optical illusions, a sophisticated design technique centuries ahead of its time.

Ellora Caves (Kailasa Temple), India

No bricks were laid, and no mortar was mixed in the creation of the Kailasa Temple at Ellora. It was created entirely by removing a volcanic cliff in India’s western state of Maharashtra. Commissioned in the 8th century AD during the Rashtrakuta dynasty, this sprawling complex (Cave 16) is the largest monolithic rock excavation on Earth. Master carvers worked top-down into a solid basalt hill, excavating over 200,000 tons of rock to reveal a multi-story temple complete with freestanding gateways, courtyard pillars and intricate sculptural friezes. Standing in its shadow means witnessing building logic completely reversed: architecture created not through construction, but pure extraction.

The Step Pyramid of Djoser, Egypt

Long before the smooth-sided giant pyramids dominated Giza, Egyptian monumental architecture began 30 kilometres south at the ancient royal necropolis of Saqqara. It was here, around 2660 BC, that Imhotep, history’s first named architect, designed the Step Pyramid of Djoser, marking humanity's transition from perishable mud-brick tombs to eternal stone construction. Imhotep originally planned a traditional flat mastaba tomb before making the bold design choice to stack six stone platforms upward, creating a 200-foot stepped silhouette. Enclosed within a 40-acre walled complex of fluted stone columns and courtyards, it serves as the prototype for all monumental stone structures that followed.

Karahan Tepe, Türkiye

Just 30 kilometres from Göbekli Tepe, Karahan Tepe proves that humanity's earliest architectural experiment was part of a far broader, interconnected landscape known as the Taş Tepeler (Stone Hills) network. Excavations here have brought to light subterranean chambers featuring standing T-shaped pillars and circular bedrock enclosures carved long before urban civilisation took root. Recently, the site made headlines with the unearthing of a striking 11,000-year-old sculpture depicting a human figure riding a leopard, alongside intact rectangular living quarters. Walking along its elevated boardwalks offers visitors an unmissable look down into native limestone enclosures defined by high-relief carvings of boars, foxes and lethal vipers.
